records.found: One unreviewed preprint posted on 2026-11-04 (Mostafaei, Hägg and colleagues, Research Square) reports that blood-based measures of biological age added a little to the prediction of death beyond age and the usual risk factors in two groups, 9,617 people in Sweden and 314,064 in the UK Biobank. It is a preprint, its measures are built from routine blood tests and not from the marks on DNA, and it is not a regulator's clearance or a health system's practice, so no rung is met. No clearance or published routine use of a clock turned up in the window.

findings.what: Preprint, not peer reviewed: 'Biological aging measures for all-cause mortality prediction in two population-based cohorts' (Mostafaei, Lindh, Qin, Mak, Hägg). In TwinGene (9,617 people) and the UK Biobank (314,064), each standard-deviation rise in several blood-based biological age measures went with 11 to 40 per cent more deaths after allowing for age, sex and other factors; adding three measures raised the prediction score from 0.780 to 0.787 and from 0.720 to 0.746.

Peer-reviewed report (Biological Psychiatry, online 2026-11-07) linking post-traumatic stress disorder to older readings on DNA-mark clocks in 43,155 United States veterans. It is about what goes with an older clock reading, not about a clock predicting death or disease, so it does not bear on the test; listed only because it is the largest clock study dated in the window. Title read, abstract not opened.

records.found: On 2026-11-06 the trial registry first posted VITAL-H (NCT07923630), a federally funded 1,200-person trial whose team has said it wants the regulator to recognise a measure of function in ageing as an endpoint; the entry records no agreement by a regulator, so the first-human test is not met. Also for the author, from before the window: on 2026-10-01 and 2026-10-02 trade reports said United States regulator officials told a Boston meeting that ageing will be a topic in the agency's next regulatory science priorities document, due early in its financial year 2027; the records hold none of this. No marker of ageing was qualified in the window.

findings.what: The trial registry first posted VITAL-H (NCT07923630, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, with the Department of Health and Human Services as collaborator): a phase 2b placebo-controlled trial of dapagliflozin and oral semaglutide in 1,200 healthy adults aged 60 to 75 over 36 months, not yet recruiting, start estimated 2027-01. Its main measure is a physical performance test score; overall intrinsic capacity, a composite of physical and mental function, is an exploratory measure. The entry records no agreement by a regulator to any measure.

Older fact the records lack. The university's release on the same trial: up to 38 million dollars over five years from the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H), 726 adults in their 60s, and three drugs including rapamycin; the lead investigator said the goal is for the regulator to recognise intrinsic capacity as an endpoint. The registry entry of 2026-11-06 differs: two drugs, no rapamycin, 1,200 people.

Older fact the entry lacks. Trade report of a panel of four United States regulator officials at the Aging Research & Drug Discovery meeting in Boston: the agency's chief scientist, Steven Kozlowski, said the next edition of its Focus Areas of Regulatory Science document will include ageing and longevity, and called for a shared, qualified endpoint for ageing trials; the panel set out how a stand-in marker would have to be validated and promised no ageing indication. Reported by a trade site, not an official transcript.

Older fact the entry lacks. Second report of the same panel (Genetic Engineering & Biotechnology News): the updated document is expected early in the regulator's financial year 2027 (which began on 2026-10-01), with no date given; Jeffrey Siegel described two possible routes for a treatment aimed at ageing, and Justin Penzenstadler expected the field to start with hard outcomes and then validate markers that predict death so trials can be shortened.

records.found: No peer-reviewed trial report dated 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-09 shows a treatment moving a clock under a plan made in advance, and no approval or published practice rests on a clock. Two trials that name a clock as an aim reached or changed on the registry (a microbe-transfer trial first posted 2026-11-03 and a tirzepatide study updated 2026-11-02), and one preprint of 2026-11-04 reported exploratory clock readings in 34 people from a food-supplement trial, none of which held after correction for multiple tests.

findings.what: The trial registry first posted NCT07912164 (sponsor Human Biome S.A.): a placebo-controlled trial of capsules of gut microbes from donors in 68 adults aged 45 to 80, not yet recruiting, start estimated 2026-12 and main results 2027-12. The entry's first question is whether the capsules slow the pace of ageing as read by the DunedinPACE clock; its main measure is the share of people who respond on clinical and biological measures at 13 and 26 weeks.

The trial registry updated NCT07906041 (first posted 2026-10-30; Atria Research and Global Health Institute with Vero Bioscience): a 22-person phase 2 feasibility study of tirzepatide whose main measure is the change over six months in a brain age read from blood proteins. It is randomised but has no masking and no placebo is listed, and it is enrolling by invitation.

Preprint, not peer reviewed (White and colleagues, medRxiv): a placebo-controlled trial of a buckwheat sprout powder in 848 adults missed its main measure of thinking; exploratory clock analyses in 34 people found signals in epigenetic age that the authors call hypothesis-generating, none surviving correction for multiple tests. Not planned in advance as a clock result and not peer reviewed, so it does not bear on the rung.

A preprint of 2026-11-02 describes a 30-protein age signature tied to heart disease risk in two groups of older adults, and on 2026-11-02 the registry updated a small tirzepatide study whose main measure is a brain age read from blood proteins with a company's organ-age test. For the author, an older paper the entry does not cite: the Stanford organ clocks were tested in 6,235 people of the Whitehall II study followed for 20 years (Kivimäki and colleagues, The Lancet Digital Health, 2025-03-01).

findings.what: Preprint, not peer reviewed (Baechle, Furman and colleagues, bioRxiv): a 30-protein signature of age built from immune proteins in blood, in two independent groups of older adults, said to track the risk of two kinds of heart disease and death. The abstract gives no group sizes and it is one signature for the heart and vessels, not an age for each of several organs.

The trial registry updated NCT07906041 (first posted 2026-10-30; Atria Research and Global Health Institute with Vero Bioscience): a 22-person phase 2 feasibility study of tirzepatide whose main measure is the change over six months in a brain age read from blood proteins. It is randomised but has no masking and no placebo is listed, and it is enrolling by invitation.

Older fact the records lack. Company release by Vero Bioscience and Atria Health and Research Institute announcing the tirzepatide study above; the release says the collaboration is a step towards clinical validation of the company's OrganAge blood test, invites readers to seek early access, and makes no claim of a regulator's clearance or routine use.

Older fact the entry lacks. Kivimäki and colleagues, The Lancet Digital Health: age gaps for nine organs, read with the Stanford group's published method, in 6,235 people aged 45 to 69 in the Whitehall II study followed for about 20 years; large gaps went with a higher risk of 30 diseases after allowing for age and sex. Two of the Stanford authors are co-authors, so it is a separate group of people but not a wholly separate team. It bears on the open question in the notes of whether two independent groups of a thousand people exist, and from when. Abstract read on Europe PMC.

records.found: On 2026-11-07 the full results of the ZEUS trial of ziltivekimab were presented at the American Heart Association meeting in Chicago and published the same day in the New England Journal of Medicine: in 6,376 people the drug lowered inflammation but not heart attacks, strokes or cardiovascular deaths (17.6 against 17.7 per cent; hazard ratio 0.99, 95% range 0.88 to 1.11), with more serious infections (20.4 against 17.9 per cent). The records hold only the company's announcement of 2026-07-31, so the second mark against is now a peer-reviewed report. It bears on the estimate towards later and less certain wide use of drugs acting on inflammation alone, because the largest test since 2017 found no benefit and some harm; the trial's own authors still name low-dose colchicine as the proven choice, so the effect on colchicine's uptake is indirect.

findings.what: Peer-reviewed trial report: Ridker and colleagues, 'Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease', New England Journal of Medicine, online 2026-11-07 (date and title confirmed in the Crossref record; the journal's own page refused the request, so the figures are from the two news reports below). No reduction in heart attacks, strokes or cardiovascular deaths against placebo.

News report of the presentation (Healio): 6,376 adults with hardened arteries, chronic kidney disease and raised inflammation; main outcome in 17.6 per cent on the drug and 17.7 per cent on placebo, hazard ratio 0.99 (0.88 to 1.11), P = 0.84; serious infections 20.4 against 17.9 per cent. The meeting ran 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-09. Two more trials of the drug, HERMES and ARTEMIS, are described as continuing.
Second news report (HCPLive): 3,184 people on the drug and 3,192 on placebo followed for a median of 33 months; 561 against 565 events; deaths from infection 3.2 against 2.5 per cent.

Hospital release (Mass General Brigham, on EurekAlert): gives the journal reference; the lead author is quoted that this drug in this setting did not work, and the authors point to low-dose colchicine as a proven option for stable disease and to targets further upstream as a possible next step.

Company announcement of nine-month results (Novo Nordisk, 07:30 Central European Time): the quarter carried a non-cash write-down of 4.6 billion Danish kroner related to ziltivekimab. The announcement as opened names no trial.

Not confirmed. A search summary said the company's full nine-month report (file dated 2026-11-03) refers to two ziltivekimab trials, HERMES and ATHENA, being discontinued. The file could not be read as text here, and the Healio report of 2026-11-07 describes HERMES as continuing. The author should read the report's pipeline pages before using this.

Peer-reviewed trial report (Baldwin and colleagues, Cardiovascular Research, online 2026-11-07): in 111 people with long-standing coronary artery disease, low-dose colchicine for 24 weeks did not lower inflammation of the main artery on scans against placebo (P = 0.38), the trial's main measure; a blood marker of inflammation fell and blood pressure rose less in secondary analyses. A small trial of how the drug works, not of heart attacks.

The trial registry first posted TARGET-CHD (NCT07920133, Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Hangzhou): 1,768 people with coronary artery disease after a stent, comparing two targets for a blood marker of inflammation to guide the colchicine dose, counting cardiovascular deaths, heart attacks and strokes over 18 months; not yet recruiting.

The trial registry updated NCT07783802 (Eli Lilly): a phase 2b placebo-controlled trial of clazakizumab, another antibody against interleukin-6, in 120 adults with raised inflammation at risk of heart disease; recruiting, main measure the fall in a blood marker of inflammation at 12 weeks, main results estimated 2027-05.

The trial registry updated NCT06263244 (Amsterdam university hospital): a 40-person placebo-controlled imaging trial of ziltivekimab is now marked completed (main completion 2026-10-30); no results posted.

records.found: On 2026-11-03 the trial registry first posted NCT07912164 (sponsor Human Biome S.A.): a placebo-controlled trial of capsules of donor gut microbes in 68 adults aged 45 to 80, set up to ask whether the transfer slows the pace of ageing on a clock and lowers inflammation, with a start estimated for 2026-12 and main results for 2027-12. It is the kind of trial the first-human rung asks for, but it has not started and has no results, so the test is not met. For the author, an older trial the records lack: ARMOR (NCT06649981), 80 adults in a placebo-controlled trial of capsules from young donors, was marked active and no longer recruiting on 2026-07-29 with its main completion dated 2026-06-17.

findings.what: The trial registry first posted NCT07912164 (sponsor Human Biome S.A.): a placebo-controlled trial of capsules of gut microbes from donors in 68 adults aged 45 to 80, not yet recruiting, start estimated 2026-12 and main results 2027-12. The entry's first question is whether the capsules slow the pace of ageing as read by the DunedinPACE clock; its main measure is the share of people who respond on clinical and biological measures at 13 and 26 weeks.

Older fact the records lack. The registry entry for ARMOR, 'Aging Resilience Through Microbiota Optimization and Regulation' (NCT06649981, 80 people): active, not recruiting, main completion 2026-06-17, last updated 2026-07-29, no results posted. A search summary describes it as a placebo-controlled trial of capsules from young, active donors in adults aged 65 to 84, measuring independence and muscle strength; that description was not read on the registry page.

unmatched.what: Peer-reviewed report (Stewart and Fitzsimmons, GeroScience): in United States transplant registry data, 4,885 kidney transplant recipients prescribed rapamycin and 6,589 not prescribed it, followed for a median of 11 years, had the same median age at death after adjustment (64.6 against 64.3 years; 95% range of the difference, 1.6 years shorter to 2.0 years longer).
unmatched.why_it_matters: One of the largest sets of people on long-term rapamycin shows no longer life, a result against the best-known candidate drug for slowing ageing; it is in transplant patients on other drugs, not healthy people.

unmatched.what: The trial registry updated NCT04264897, the 'Antecedent Metabolic Health and Metformin Aging Study' (Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation with the National Institute on Aging; 166 people without diabetes, metformin against placebo for 12 weeks; completed, results first posted 2026-07-02). The posted analyses of its two main measures, insulin sensitivity and a measure of mitochondrial function, give P values of 0.576 and 0.88.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A placebo-controlled test of whether metformin helps people without diabetes, the question behind the metformin ageing trial; the posted results show no clear effect on its main measures. The results themselves predate the window.

unmatched.what: Peer-reviewed design paper for AMICO (journal COPD): a phase 3 placebo-controlled trial of metformin over 36 months in 212 people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, described by its authors as testing metformin as a treatment aimed at ageing in that disease.
unmatched.why_it_matters: A phase 3 trial that frames an old drug as an ageing treatment inside one disease; also listed under the regulator record, where it does not meet the test.
